title: Why Germany's 1848 Revolution Won Everything, Then Lost It
description:
In March 1848 the German revolution won almost everywhere: princes gave way, censorship ended, and Germany's first freely elected parliament met in Frankfurt's St Paul's Church. Sixteen months later the last revolutionaries surrendered at the fortress of Rastatt. Why?

This explainer walks through the map Germany started from in 1815, what liberals and democrats actually wanted, the Schleswig-Holstein war, the impossible choice between a Greater and a Lesser Germany, the crown Friedrich Wilhelm IV refused, and the Prussian campaigns of 1849, with animated maps for every step. It ends with the Forty-Eighters who emigrated to America and the Frankfurt constitution's afterlife in 1919 and 1949.

scenes.narration: In the spring of 1848, revolution swept Europe. Paris rose in February; within a month, Vienna, Budapest, Milan and Berlin followed. Across the German states, rulers gave way. By May, an elected German parliament sat in Frankfurt. Little more than a year later, all of it was gone. So why did a revolution that won almost everywhere in March 1848 lose everything by July 1849?

visuals.text: Won in March, Lost by July

scenes.narration: The answer has three parts: the map Germany started from, the revolutionaries' own divisions, and two great powers waiting to recover. We start in 1815. That year the Congress of Vienna created not a Germany but the German Confederation: thirty-nine states. Its only common body was a Federal Diet of princes' envoys in Frankfurt. There was no German government, no German army, no German citizenship. Two members were giants, Prussia and Austria, and both ruled large lands outside the Confederation. Austria's empire included Hungarians, Czechs, Poles, Croats and Italians. That will decide the ending.

visuals.subtext: at its founding by the Congress of Vienna, 1815

scenes.narration: Austria's chancellor, Prince Metternich, guarded this order. He feared two ideas: liberalism, meaning constitutions and a free press, and nationalism, the idea of one German state. Both threatened a multinational empire like his. From 1819, the Carlsbad Decrees put universities under watch and newspapers under censorship. When tens of thousands rallied at Hambach in 1832 under black, red and gold, the Diet answered with more repression.

visuals.subtext: Austrian chancellor, architect of the 1815 order

scenes.narration: The pressure was economic too. Machine-made cloth, much of it British, undercut home weavers. In 1844, Silesian weavers rose, and Prussian troops shot eleven of them. Then came hunger. Potato blight struck in 1845, and the harvest of 1846 failed. In April 1847, hungry Berliners stormed market stalls: the Potato Revolution. Liberals wanted rights and a nation; craftsmen, labourers and peasants wanted bread, work and an end to feudal dues. In March they fought side by side.

The spark came from Paris. In late February 1848, after three days of street fighting, the king abdicated and France became a republic. Three days later, a meeting in Mannheim drew up four demands: arming of the people, unconditional freedom of the press, trial by jury, and the immediate creation of a German parliament. These became the March demands.

The princes gave in fast. Baden, Württemberg, Hesse, Saxony and Hanover got liberal March ministries. In Bavaria, the king abdicated. Then came the two capitals that mattered. In Vienna, on the thirteenth of March, troops fired on demonstrators. That evening Metternich resigned. He fled into exile in England.

Five days later, Berlin. On the eighteenth of March, two shots went off outside the royal palace, most probably by accident. Within hours, Berliners built more than nine hundred barricades, by one count. More than two hundred civilians died, and fewer than fifty soldiers. The next day, King Friedrich Wilhelm the Fourth withdrew his troops. Days later he rode through Berlin wearing black, red and gold.

scenes.narration: By the end of March, even the old Federal Diet had adopted black, red and gold. Next came the fourth demand: a national parliament. Elections followed across the Confederation, under rules that varied by state. Deputies came to Frankfurt from Königsberg to Trieste. On the eighteenth of May 1848, they walked in procession into St Paul's Church.

visuals.caption: Deputies enter St Paul's Church, Frankfurt, 18 May 1848

scenes.narration: The Assembly had about five hundred and eighty-five seats. Counting substitutes, around eight hundred men served. Most were judges, civil servants, lawyers and professors; one historian counted not a single worker. People called it the professors' parliament. Its president was Heinrich von Gagern, a Hessian liberal who wanted a constitutional monarchy.

scenes.narration: It was divided from the start. Liberals like Gagern wanted a constitutional monarchy, built with the princes. Democrats wanted popular sovereignty, an equal vote for all men, often a republic. Some were ready to fight. One of them, the Mannheim lawyer Friedrich Hecker, had not waited for Frankfurt.

In April 1848 he set out from Konstanz to march on Karlsruhe and declare a republic. He expected tens of thousands. His column wound west through the Black Forest. Near Kandern, government troops scattered his roughly one thousand men. The general killed that day was Friedrich von Gagern, older brother of the future parliament president. Hecker fled to Switzerland.

The first test came in the north. Schleswig and Holstein were ruled by the Danish king, but only Holstein was in the Confederation. When Danish nationalists moved to bind Schleswig to Denmark, Germans there revolted, and Frankfurt backed them. But Frankfurt had no army, so Prussian troops marched into Schleswig for it. Then, under great-power pressure, Prussia signed an armistice at Malmö without asking Frankfurt. The Assembly first rejected it, then gave in. In September crowds rose in Frankfurt, two conservative deputies were killed, and Prussian and Austrian troops from Mainz restored order.

By autumn, the old powers had their armies back, and they used them. In October, Vienna rose again. Prince Windischgrätz, who had crushed Prague in June, stormed the city with Croatian troops under Jelačić. Among the defenders was Robert Blum, a leader of the Frankfurt left. He claimed immunity as a deputy. On the ninth of November he was shot. The next day, General Wrangel marched Prussian troops back into Berlin. In December the king imposed his own constitution.

visuals.file: File:Portrait of Robert Blum by August Hunger.jpg

scenes.narration: Now the hardest question: where was Germany? A Greater Germany would include Austria. But only Austria's German lands and Bohemia were in the Confederation. Hungary, Galicia and northern Italy were not. Including Austria meant splitting its empire. Vienna refused. In March 1849 it bound the whole empire, Hungary included, into one state. That left a Lesser Germany, without Austria, led by the King of Prussia.

In December 1848 the Assembly passed the Basic Rights: equality before the law, freedom of the press, of religion and of assembly, and the abolition of the death penalty, with exceptions. In March 1849 came the constitution: a federal empire, an elected parliament, a hereditary emperor. The Assembly then elected Friedrich Wilhelm the Fourth emperor: two hundred and ninety votes for, two hundred and forty-eight abstentions.

scenes.narration: On the third of April 1849, deputies led by Eduard Simson offered him the crown in Berlin. He stalled, and within weeks refused outright. Privately he had called it an imaginary hoop baked out of mud and clay. A king by the grace of God would not take a crown from a parliament. Austria and the larger kingdoms rejected the constitution. Twenty-eight smaller governments accepted it. Frankfurt had a constitution, and no power to enforce it.

visuals.caption: The Frankfurt delegation before Friedrich Wilhelm IV, Berlin, 3 April 1849

visuals.text: Such an imaginary hoop, baked out of mud and clay …
visuals.subtext: Friedrich Wilhelm IV, private letter to Christian von Bunsen, 13 December 1848 (translated)

scenes.narration: In May 1849, democrats rose to force the princes to accept it: the Reich Constitution Campaign. Dresden fought for a week, with Richard Wagner among the rebels. Elberfeld and Iserlohn rose in Prussia's west. In the Palatinate, revolutionaries took over. In Baden the army changed sides: Rastatt's garrison mutinied and the Grand Duke fled. The parliament's rump moved to Stuttgart, where troops dispersed it in June.

Each time, Prussia answered. Its troops helped retake Dresden. Then two Prussian corps under the king's brother, Prince Wilhelm, cleared the Palatinate, crossed the Rhine at Germersheim and beat the Baden army at Waghäusel. The rebels fell back behind the Murg, then into Rastatt. Besieged from late June, the fortress surrendered on the twenty-third of July 1849. Courts martial followed. Twenty-seven men were executed in Baden.

One of Rastatt's defenders was a twenty-year-old student, Carl Schurz. He escaped through an unguarded sewer, crossed the Rhine to France and reached Switzerland. About eighty thousand people left Baden after the revolution, most for America, driven mostly by poverty, some by politics. German emigration to America peaked in 1854: over two hundred and fifteen thousand in one year. These exiles were the Forty-Eighters. Hecker led Union regiments in the Civil War; Schurz became a Union general and a senator for Missouri.

scenes.narration: So why did March 1848 end at Rastatt, sixteen months later? Three reasons. First, power. In March the princes lost their nerve, not their armies. Once Austria and Prussia had their soldiers back, Frankfurt had nothing to set against them. Second, division. Liberals wanted order and a monarchy, democrats a republic, and many liberals came to fear the street more than the kings. Third, geography. No one could agree where Germany was. Austria could not join without breaking its empire, nor simply be left out.

Germany was united in 1871 by Prussian arms, without Austria, under that same Prince Wilhelm, now emperor: the Lesser German map, without the Frankfurt freedoms. Those freedoms returned. In 1919 the Weimar Republic adopted black, red and gold and drew on the Frankfurt basic rights; so did West Germany's Basic Law in 1949. Article twenty-two still names black, red and gold as the federal flag. The revolution lost in 1849. Its constitution became a model for German democracy.
